subject: system-design
title: Publish-Subscribe
summary: A one-to-many fan-out pattern where publishers send to a topic and every interested subscriber gets its own copy — broadcast, not work distribution.

blocks.text: In publish-subscribe, a publisher sends a message to a named topic, and every subscriber to that topic receives its own copy. The publisher never names the recipients and doesn't know how many there are. This is one-to-many fan-out: one event, delivered to everyone who cares.

A message queue delivers each message to one consumer — work to be done once. Pub-sub delivers each message to all subscribers — an announcement everyone hears. The same 'order placed' event might be consumed once by a queue worker that charges the card, but fanned out by pub-sub to billing, shipping, and analytics, each getting its own copy.

A broker sits in the middle and a topic is the channel on it. Publishers write to a topic, subscribers read from it, and neither side knows the other exists. That indirection is the value: you can add a new subscriber to an event stream without touching, or even notifying, the publisher.

items: Push: the broker actively delivers messages to subscribers as they arrive — low latency, but it can overwhelm a slow subscriber.
Pull: subscribers fetch on their own schedule — they control the pace, at the cost of some delay.
Pull also makes it natural to replay or catch up after a subscriber has been offline.
Event-driven systems: services react to events instead of calling each other directly.
Notifications: one action fans out to email, push, and in-app channels.
Fan-out to many services: a single event feeds search indexing, caches, and audit logs at once.

blocks.text: Pub-sub carries the same delivery semantics as queues — at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once — and at-least-once with idempotent subscribers is again the common choice. But subscribers can be slow or absent, so the broker must decide what to do: buffer messages for later, expire them after a retention window, or drop them for a subscriber that has fallen too far behind.

blocks.title: Pub-sub vs a message queue
blocks.text: Reach for pub-sub when many independent consumers each need the same event (broadcast). Reach for a queue when one piece of work should be done once by whichever worker is free (point-to-point work distribution).
